stages.instruction:
Master the building blocks of the web. HTML structures content, CSS styles and positions it, JavaScript makes it interactive.

OBJECTIVE
Build and style a real web page with semantic HTML, CSS layout, and responsive behaviour.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Write semantic HTML landmarks and forms
• Lay out content with Flexbox and CSS Grid
• Make the page usable from 375px to desktop without horizontal scrolling

WORKED EXAMPLE
Build a responsive pricing card. Step 1: structure the markup semantically — `<section>`, `<h2>`, a `<ul>` of features and an `<a>` action. Step 2: apply a single-column flex layout with a max-width. Step 3: add `@media (min-width: 640px)` that switches to a row. Step 4: check 375px and 1280px — the card must never cause horizontal scroll and every control must be keyboard reachable.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Using <div> for everything instead of semantic elements like <nav>, <main> and <section>
• Fighting layout with fixed pixel widths instead of Flexbox or Grid
• Forgetting the viewport meta tag, so mobile browsers zoom out

stages.instruction:
Go deep into JavaScript. Learn modern syntax, DOM manipulation, and how to fetch data from APIs.

OBJECTIVE
Manipulate the DOM and handle asynchronous data with modern JavaScript.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Select and update DOM elements safely
• Handle user events and form submission
• Fetch data with async/await and handle success and failure states

WORKED EXAMPLE
Filter and render a product list. Step 1: hold the raw `products` array and a `maxPrice` value. Step 2: derive results with `const visible = products.filter((p) => p.inStock && p.price <= maxPrice)`. Step 3: render each item with `.map()` into template strings and `join("")`. Step 4: log `visible` before rendering to confirm the transform. Notice the derived data is computed, never mutated.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Forgetting that fetch() only rejects on network failure — check response.ok for 4xx/5xx
• Reassigning a const binding
• Ignoring rapid input, so out-of-order responses overwrite newer results

success_criteria: Render lists and handle user input in React
stages.instruction:
React is the most in-demand frontend skill. Build component-based UIs and production apps with Next.js.

OBJECTIVE
Build component-based interfaces with React and understand how state and props drive rendering.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Compose components with props
• Manage state with hooks
• Render lists and handle user input in React

WORKED EXAMPLE
Add a searchable list in React. Step 1: hold `query` in `useState`. Step 2: derive `const results = useMemo(() => items.filter((i) => i.name.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase())), [items, query])`. Step 3: bind the input to `query` and render `results`. Step 4: type in the box and confirm results change without `items` being modified — if it changes, you are mutating state.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Mutating state directly instead of using the setter
• Missing the key prop when rendering lists
• Running side effects in the render body instead of useEffect

stages.objective: Apply the professional practices that make frontend work maintainable: version control, testing, performance, accessibility and deployment.
stages.instruction:
Bridge the gap from learning to professional work. These are the practices that separate juniors from team-ready developers.

OBJECTIVE
Apply the professional practices that make frontend work maintainable: version control, testing, performance, accessibility and deployment.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Use a branching Git workflow
• Write component tests
• Meet basic accessibility requirements
• Deploy to a hosting platform

WORKED EXAMPLE
Debug a failing test. Step 1: read the assertion message and reproduce the failure locally. Step 2: reduce the input to the smallest case that still fails. Step 3: form one hypothesis and change one thing only. Step 4: re-run. If it passes, commit with a message stating the cause; if not, revert before trying the next hypothesis so you never stack unrelated changes.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Treating accessibility as optional
• Committing directly to main with no review
• Shipping without testing the production build

stages.instruction:
Use AI as a powerful assistant, not a replacement for understanding. Build faster without losing the ability to think.

OBJECTIVE
Use AI tools as assistants while keeping ownership of correctness and architecture.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Generate useful boilerplate with AI
• Review and correct AI output
• Explain the code you ship

WORKED EXAMPLE
Use AI to scaffold, then own the result. Step 1: prompt for a small component with explicit requirements. Step 2: read every line it returns and look for invented props or imports. Step 3: fix accessibility (labels, focus, contrast) and add one test. Step 4: if you cannot explain a line, delete it and rewrite it yourself — the AI draft is input, not the deliverable.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Shipping generated code without reading it
• Trusting AI explanations of unfamiliar APIs
• Letting AI make architectural decisions

stages.instruction:
Understand how web servers communicate and pick your first backend language.

OBJECTIVE
Explain how the web works and run a first backend program with HTTP and version control.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Describe the request/response cycle
• Run a minimal server or script
• Use Git and a terminal confidently

WORKED EXAMPLE
Handle a request cleanly. Step 1: read the method, path and body. Step 2: validate the body against a schema and reject invalid input early. Step 3: call a service function that contains the business logic. Step 4: map the result or a domain error to a status code (400/404/409/500) and return JSON. Keep validation and logic out of the route handler.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Confusing HTTP methods with actions
• Committing secrets or node_modules
• Not understanding that the server is stateless between requests

stages.instruction:
Build real APIs. Handle requests, manage authentication, and structure your application cleanly.

OBJECTIVE
Design and implement a REST API with authentication, validation and correct error handling.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Design resource-oriented routes
• Hash passwords and issue tokens
• Validate input and return correct status codes

WORKED EXAMPLE
Design `POST /orders`. Step 1: define the request schema (items, quantities, customer). Step 2: reject an empty cart with 422 and a field-level message. Step 3: create the order and return 201 with a `Location` header pointing at the new resource. Step 4: accept a client-supplied idempotency key so a retried request does not create a duplicate order.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Storing passwords in plain text
• Returning 200 for errors
• Trusting client-supplied data without validation

stages.instruction:
Data is the heart of every application. Design schemas, query efficiently, and connect databases to your APIs.

OBJECTIVE
Model data and query a relational database safely and efficiently.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Design normalised tables with keys
• Write SELECTs with joins and aggregation
• Explain an index and when it helps

WORKED EXAMPLE
Model orders and line items. Step 1: create `users`, then `orders` with a foreign key to `users`. Step 2: create `order_items` referencing both `orders` and a `products` table. Step 3: add indexes on the foreign-key columns and on the column you filter by. Step 4: run `EXPLAIN` on your main query and confirm it uses the index rather than a full scan.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Storing duplicate data across tables
• Using SELECT * in production queries
• Assuming an index always helps — it slows writes and adds storage

stages.instruction:
Level up your APIs with performance patterns and real-time features.

OBJECTIVE
Apply advanced backend patterns: caching, background work, real-time transport and rate limiting.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Explain when to cache
• Move slow work to a background job
• Choose the right transport for real-time features
• Protect endpoints with rate limiting

WORKED EXAMPLE
Add caching to a read endpoint. Step 1: build a cache key from the input (path + query). Step 2: check the cache; on a hit, return immediately. Step 3: on a miss, query the database, store the result with a TTL, and return it. Step 4: on any write that affects the data, invalidate the matching key. Verify a second identical read is served from cache.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Caching data that must always be fresh
• Doing CPU-heavy work inside a request
• Adding WebSockets where polling was sufficient

stages.instruction:
Get your APIs live. Learn containerization and deployment pipelines.

OBJECTIVE
Containerise, configure and deploy a backend service with a repeatable pipeline.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Containerise an app with Docker
• Manage configuration with environment variables
• Deploy with a CI/CD pipeline

WORKED EXAMPLE
Containerise and deploy the API. Step 1: write a multi-stage Dockerfile that builds then runs as a non-root user. Step 2: pass all configuration through environment variables and document each one. Step 3: add a `/health` route. Step 4: run database migrations as a release step, not at container start-up, and confirm the app boots from a clean environment using only the documented variables.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Baking secrets into the image
• Using a huge base image
• Deploying without running tests first

Deploy a working frontend to a hosting platform
stages.instruction:
Full-stack starts with frontend mastery. Complete the Frontend Development track in full first.

OBJECTIVE
Build and deploy a responsive frontend before you add a backend.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Build a responsive UI with React and Tailwind CSS
• Deploy a working frontend to a hosting platform

WORKED EXAMPLE
Build the frontend half faithfully. Step 1: follow the design's structure with semantic HTML. Step 2: lay it out so it holds at 375px and 1280px. Step 3: wire one interactive element to component state. Step 4: keep the data-fetching seam obvious — a single module — so you can swap mocks for the real API later.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Leaving deployment until the very end
• Only testing on a desktop browser width

stages.instruction:
Then complete the Backend Development track, especially REST APIs, authentication, and PostgreSQL.

OBJECTIVE
Consolidate the backend skills you will connect to the frontend: APIs, databases and authentication.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Expose a REST API with correct status codes

Build and document the API. Step 1: define the endpoints and their status codes. Step 2: add request validation. Step 3: persist to a database through a repository layer. Step 4: call every endpoint from a client script and add a request log — do not trust the route file alone.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Storing secrets in source control
• Trusting client input without server-side validation

• Assuming the client can be trusted for authorization

questions.question: A browser request to your API is blocked by CORS. What is the correct fix?
options: Disable the browser security
Configure the server to send the appropriate Access-Control-Allow-* headers for the allowed origin
Rename the endpoint
Use HTTP instead of HTTPS
questions.correct_option: Configure the server to send the appropriate Access-Control-Allow-* headers for the allowed origin
questions.explanation: CORS is enforced by the browser; the server must grant access with the correct response headers.

questions.question: Where must an authorization decision be enforced for trust?
options: In the browser UI only
On the server for every request
In CSS
In the database client
questions.correct_option: On the server for every request
questions.explanation: The server is the trust boundary; client checks are only for user experience.

questions.question: What is an optimistic UI update?
options: Updating the UI immediately and rolling back if the server request fails
Waiting for the server before showing anything
Never showing errors
Caching every response forever
questions.correct_option: Updating the UI immediately and rolling back if the server request fails
questions.explanation: Optimistic updates feel fast but must roll back when the server rejects the change.

stages.instruction:
Get the complete stack live. Managing different deployment environments is a real skill.

OBJECTIVE
Deploy the frontend, backend and database together and manage configuration safely.

SUCCESS CRITERIA

• Sharing one database URL between development and production
• Committing a populated .env file

Use a separate DATABASE_URL per environment
Rely on table prefixes
Disable the database in development

questions.question: Why serve the app over HTTPS?
options: It makes it faster
It encrypts traffic and verifies the server identity
It removes the need for authentication
It compresses images

questions.question: A deploy works locally but fails in production because an environment variable is missing. How do you prevent this?

questions.question: Why must a payment webhook signature be verified on the server?
options: To make it faster
To prove the notification genuinely came from the payment provider
To avoid storing data
To reduce cost
questions.correct_option: To prove the notification genuinely came from the payment provider
questions.explanation: An unverified webhook can be forged, letting an attacker grant themselves paid access.

questions.question: When should work be moved to a background job?
options: When it is quick and must block the response
When it is long-running or does not need to block the user response
Never
Only on the client
questions.correct_option: When it is long-running or does not need to block the user response
questions.explanation: Long or non-urgent work belongs in the background so requests stay fast and reliable.

questions.question: Why is idempotency important in payment handling?
options: It makes payments free
So retries do not charge or credit the same order twice
It speeds up the database
It encrypts the card
questions.correct_option: So retries do not charge or credit the same order twice
questions.explanation: Webhooks and network retries can repeat an event; idempotent handling prevents duplicate effects.

Python is one of the easiest languages to start with. Nail the fundamentals and everything else opens up.

OBJECTIVE
Write clear Python programs using core data types, control flow, functions and file handling.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Use lists, dicts, tuples and sets appropriately
• Write functions with clear inputs and outputs

stages.instruction:
Figma is the industry-standard design tool. Learn it deeply, components, auto-layout, and interactive prototypes.

OBJECTIVE
Use Figma fluently: components, variants, auto layout, prototyping and developer handoff.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Build reusable components with variants
• Use auto layout and constraints
• Prototype interactions and prepare handoff

WORKED EXAMPLE
Build a button component in Figma. Step 1: create variants for default, hover and disabled. Step 2: use auto-layout with padding and gap tokens. Step 3: place instances on a screen. Step 4: change the variant property once and confirm every instance updates — if it does not, your instances are detached.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Detaching components constantly
• Using absolute positioning instead of auto layout
• No naming convention, so handoff is confusing

stages.instruction:

OBJECTIVE
Test designs with users and design inclusively and mobile-first.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Plan and run a usability test
• Identify and fix accessibility issues

WORKED EXAMPLE
Run a five-task usability test. Step 1: give each participant a goal, not instructions. Step 2: record completion, time and where they hesitate. Step 3: note verbatim quotes for each friction point. • Leading participants to the answer
• Testing with too few or unrepresentative users
• Treating accessibility as a final checkbox

• Testing only the happy path
• No expected result defined

OBJECTIVE
Query relational data with SQL: filtering, aggregation, joins, subqueries and window functions.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Filter and sort with WHERE/ORDER BY

WORKED EXAMPLE
Answer "top customers by revenue". Step 1: start from `orders` and join `customers` on `customer_id`. Step 2: filter to paid orders with `WHERE status = 'paid'`. COMMON MISTAKES
• Using WHERE instead of HAVING to filter aggregates
• Forgetting that LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched left rows
• Assuming NULL comparisons work with =

stages.instruction:
You need enough statistics to avoid drawing wrong conclusions from your data.

OBJECTIVE
Apply basic statistics correctly and avoid common misinterpretations.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Summarise data with appropriate measures
• Interpret spread and correlation
• Explain what a hypothesis test does and does not prove

WORKED EXAMPLE
Compare two groups. Step 1: state the null hypothesis. Step 2: check the sample sizes are adequate. Step 3: run the appropriate test and note its assumptions. Step 4: report the effect size and confidence interval — not just the p-value — and state any assumption you could not verify.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Using the mean for skewed data without checking
• Treating correlation as causation
• Reading a p-value as the probability the hypothesis is true

stages.instruction:
You do not need a math degree, but you need enough to understand why models work and when they fail.

OBJECTIVE
Understand the statistics and maths that underpin machine learning.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Describe common probability distributions
• Explain what a gradient is
• Interpret a hypothesis test correctly

WORKED EXAMPLE
Follow a gradient by hand. Step 1: pick a tiny dataset and define the loss as mean squared error. Step 2: choose two candidate weights, compute the loss for each and tabulate them. Step 3: compute the gradient — the slope of the loss with respect to the weight — and note its sign. Step 4: take a small step in the opposite direction, recompute the loss and confirm it fell. Repeat once; you have just run gradient descent, the mathematics behind model training.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Treating a p-value as the probability the hypothesis is true
• Assuming the mean works for skewed data

stages.stage_description: Build your first real screens. Mobile development feels different from web, learn the patterns that make apps feel native.
stages.objective: Build screens with navigation, state and device APIs.
success_criteria: Use a device API with permission
stages.instruction:
Build your first real screens. Mobile development feels different from web, learn the patterns that make apps feel native.

OBJECTIVE
Build screens with navigation, state and device APIs.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Navigate between screens
• Manage state
• Use a device API with permission

WORKED EXAMPLE
Build a list screen. Step 1: fetch the data on mount. Step 2: show a loading state. Step 3: render the items and handle the empty case with a message. Step 4: navigate to a detail screen on tap. Keep state local until two screens genuinely need to share it.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Blocking the UI thread with heavy work
• Forgetting to handle permission denial

stages.instruction:
Firebase gives your app a full backend without building one from scratch. Perfect for MVPs.

OBJECTIVE
Add backend services with Firebase.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Set up authentication
• Store and read data
• Use storage and notifications

WORKED EXAMPLE

COMMON MISTAKES
• Leaving database rules open
• Storing sensitive data in the client

topics: Cut types: hard cut, J-cut, L-cut
stages.objective: Cut a clean timeline with correct audio and export settings.
stages.instruction:
Learn how editing software works and the fundamental language of cuts, transitions, and timing.

OBJECTIVE
Cut a clean timeline with correct audio and export settings.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Assemble a timeline
• Use cut types deliberately
• Export a correct file

WORKED EXAMPLE
Cut a 60-second clip from raw footage. Step 1: import and trim to the best take. Step 2: add a J or L cut so the audio leads or trails the picture smoothly. Step 3: normalise audio levels. Step 4: export at the platform's target resolution and bitrate. Watch it back on a phone before exporting again.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Editing audio after picture
• Exporting at the wrong resolution or bitrate

questions.question: What is a J-cut?
options: A hard cut
Audio from the next clip starts before its picture
A cut with no transition
A cut to black

questions.question: Why level audio before final export?

So dialogue is consistently audible and nothing clips or is buried
It reduces file size
It adds captions

questions.question: A video looks soft after upload even though it looked sharp locally. What is the most likely cause?

Too much colour grading
The music choice

questions.explanation: Under-spec export settings, or platform re-encoding, can soften a video.

stages.stage_description: Technical editing is the vehicle. Storytelling is the destination. Make people watch until the end.
stages.objective: Structure an edit so viewers stay to the end.
stages.instruction:
Technical editing is the vehicle. Storytelling is the destination. Make people watch until the end.

OBJECTIVE
Structure an edit so viewers stay to the end.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Apply story structure
• Pace for the format
• Use music purposefully

WORKED EXAMPLE
Restructure a flat video. Step 1: open with the outcome rather than the setup. Step 2: add a hook in the first five seconds. Step 3: place a pattern interrupt (a cut, a question, a graphic) in the middle. Step 4: end on a clear call to action. Compare the retention curve before and after.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Slow openings that lose viewers
• Music that fights the dialogue

Each field has specific AI workflows. Learn the tools and patterns for your specific track.

OBJECTIVE
Apply AI effectively within your own field.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Use coding assistants safely
• Use AI for design/analysis
• Verify domain output

WORKED EXAMPLE
Build a workflow for your own field. Step 1: pick a recurring task in your work. Step 2: write the input template and the instruction. Step 3: define the review step and what you check before using the output. Step 4: log one failure and the correction that fixed it.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Merging AI code without review
• Trusting AI analysis of data you cannot see it computed correctly

stages.stage_description: The most important AI skill is knowing when not to trust it. Build the habit of verification.
stages.objective: Use AI responsibly with verification and privacy in mind.
stages.instruction:
The most important AI skill is knowing when not to trust it. Build the habit of verification.

OBJECTIVE
Use AI responsibly with verification and privacy in mind.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Verify outputs
• Protect private data
• Reason before prompting

WORKED EXAMPLE
Verify AI output before using it. Step 1: identify any factual claims. Step 2: check each against a primary source. Step 3: look for bias, missing context or fabricated references. Step 4: record the verification and note any claim you could not confirm.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Pasting confidential data into tools
• Publishing unverified AI output
stages.worked_example: Verify AI output before using it. Step 1: identify any factual claims. Step 2: check each against a primary source. Step 3: look for bias, missing context or fabricated references. Step 4: record the verification and note any claim you could not confirm.
common_mistakes: Pasting confidential data into tools
Publishing unverified AI output

• Ignoring breakpoints

stages.instruction:

Connect apps and services with automation.

SUCCESS CRITERIA

• Connect APIs without code

COMMON MISTAKES
• No error handling
• Automating a process that changes constantly

stages.stage_description: Good technical writing is not about big vocabulary, it is about clarity. Say complex things simply.
stages.objective: Write clearly for a technical audience.
stages.instruction:
Good technical writing is not about big vocabulary, it is about clarity. Say complex things simply.

OBJECTIVE
Write clearly for a technical audience.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Write concisely
• Use active voice
• Structure for scanning

WORKED EXAMPLE
Rewrite a dense paragraph for a defined reader. Step 1: name the reader and what they need to do. Step 2: cut filler and jargon, keeping technical meaning intact. Step 3: split long sentences and lead with the action. Step 4: compare before and after and justify your three biggest changes.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Long passive sentences
• Assuming the reader has your context
stages.worked_example: Rewrite a dense paragraph for a defined reader. Step 1: name the reader and what they need to do. Step 2: cut filler and jargon, keeping technical meaning intact. Step 3: split long sentences and lead with the action. Step 4: compare before and after and justify your three biggest changes.
common_mistakes: Long passive sentences
Assuming the reader has your context

questions.question: Which sentence is in active voice?
options: The bug was fixed by the team.
The team fixed the bug.
The bug had been fixed.
A fix was applied.
questions.correct_option: The team fixed the bug.
questions.explanation: Active voice puts the actor first: "The team fixed the bug."

questions.question: Why prefer short sentences and headings in technical writing?
options: They look nicer
Readers scan for the answer; structure helps them find it fast
They reduce word count only
They are required
questions.correct_option: Readers scan for the answer; structure helps them find it fast
questions.explanation: Structure and brevity help readers find answers quickly.

questions.question: Writing "simply click the obvious button" is a problem because…
options: It is too short
It assumes shared context and may be wrong or condescending
It uses contractions
It is passive
questions.correct_option: It assumes shared context and may be wrong or condescending
questions.explanation: Ambiguous, assumptive instructions fail for readers without your context.

brief.problem: A dense internal document is hard for its real audience to act on.
brief.audience: A named, non-expert reader who must act on the content.
brief.objective: Rewrite the source for clarity without losing accuracy.
prerequisites: None
functionalRequirements: A defined audience and purpose
A restructured version (headings, short paragraphs, examples)
Annotated justifications for the major changes
A before/after comparison
constraints: Do not change technical meaning
Keep all required information
Prefer plain language over jargon where possible
acceptanceCriteria: A reader can find the key action quickly
No factual meaning changed
At least five changes are justified
evidence: Before and after documents
An annotated list of changes and why
A short accuracy review note
commonFailureCases: Simplifying until the content is wrong
No audience definition
Changes made with no rationale

stages.objective: Implement token standards and use professional tooling.
stages.instruction:
Standards are why the ecosystem interoperates. Implement ERC-20 and ERC-721 with battle-tested libraries and a professional test-and-deploy workflow.

OBJECTIVE
Implement token standards and use professional tooling.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Distinguish ERC-20 and ERC-721
• Use OpenZeppelin
• Test and deploy a contract

WORKED EXAMPLE
Create an ERC-20 token. Step 1: define name, symbol, decimals and total supply. Step 2: add access-controlled minting. Step 3: write tests for transfer, approve and mint authorisation. Step 4: deploy to a testnet and verify the source on the explorer.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Rolling your own token logic instead of audited libraries
• Deploying to mainnet without tests

stages.objective: Explain the core mechanics of decentralised finance.
stages.instruction:
The core primitives of decentralised finance: how automated market makers price assets, how lending markets set rates, and what makes a stablecoin stable.

OBJECTIVE
Explain the core mechanics of decentralised finance.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Explain AMM pricing
• Describe liquidity and impermanent loss
• Compare stablecoin types

WORKED EXAMPLE
Build a minimal AMM. Step 1: implement the constant-product reserve formula. Step 2: add add-liquidity and swap functions. Step 3: test a swap and compute the price impact. Step 4: write down what a large trade does to the price and why.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Assuming LP fees always outweigh impermanent loss
• Treating all stablecoins as equally safe

questions.question: In a constant-product AMM (x × y = k), what happens as a trade grows large?
options: Price stays constant
The average execution price slips further from the starting price
The pool gains liquidity
Fees fall to zero
questions.correct_option: The average execution price slips further from the starting price
questions.explanation: Large trades move the pool balances more, causing greater slippage.

questions.question: What is impermanent loss?
options: A permanent fee
The loss an LP suffers versus simply holding the tokens when the pool price diverges
A hacking loss
A tax
questions.correct_option: The loss an LP suffers versus simply holding the tokens when the pool price diverges
questions.explanation: Impermanent loss is the divergence cost LPs face relative to holding.

questions.question: Which stablecoin design depends hardest on external collateral staying solvent?
options: Algorithmic, undercollateralised designs
Fully fiat-backed
Overcollateralised crypto-backed
Tokenised deposits
questions.correct_option: Algorithmic, undercollateralised designs
questions.explanation: Undercollateralised algorithmic designs are the most fragile when confidence breaks.

• Assuming bridges are as safe as the chains they connect

questions.question: What is a flash-loan attack?
options: A slow loan repaid over years
A loan taken and repaid within one transaction, used to manipulate prices or bypass checks
A hack of the wallet
A governance vote
questions.correct_option: A loan taken and repaid within one transaction, used to manipulate prices or bypass checks
questions.explanation: Flash loans require no collateral because they are borrowed and repaid in one atomic transaction.

questions.question: Why are cross-chain bridges frequent targets?
options: They are cheap to run
They concentrate large value and often rely on complex, permissioned validation
They are regulated
They hold no funds
questions.correct_option: They concentrate large value and often rely on complex, permissioned validation
questions.explanation: Bridges hold large value and add trust assumptions and complex code, raising risk.

questions.question: What is MEV?
options: A wallet standard
Value extracted by reordering, inserting or censoring transactions in a block
A type of token
A consensus algorithm
questions.correct_option: Value extracted by reordering, inserting or censoring transactions in a block
questions.explanation: MEV is value captured through transaction ordering within blocks.

stages.objective: Use indexing and decentralised storage in a dApp.
stages.instruction:
Indexing and storage are what make dApps usable at scale. Query historical data with The Graph and store assets on IPFS.

OBJECTIVE
Use indexing and decentralised storage in a dApp.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Query indexed data
• Store files on IPFS
• Assemble a full dApp

WORKED EXAMPLE
Store and retrieve dApp data. Step 1: decide what belongs on-chain (state) versus off-chain (large files). Step 2: write on-chain state with events. Step 3: store metadata on IPFS and reference its hash on-chain. Step 4: read the state back and confirm the hash resolves.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Scanning every block for history in the frontend
• Assuming IPFS guarantees persistence without pinning

questions.question: Why use The Graph instead of reading events directly from a node?
options: It is prettier
It indexes blockchain data so historical queries are fast and simple
It stores private keys
It mines tokens
questions.correct_option: It indexes blockchain data so historical queries are fast and simple
questions.explanation: The Graph indexes events into queryable data, avoiding slow block scans.

questions.question: What does IPFS content addressing mean?
options: Files are stored on one server
A file is referenced by a hash of its content
Files are encrypted
Files are free forever
questions.correct_option: A file is referenced by a hash of its content
questions.explanation: IPFS addresses content by hash, so identical content shares an address.

questions.question: A file is added to IPFS but later becomes unavailable. Why?
options: It never uploaded
IPFS does not guarantee persistence unless the content is pinned/replicated
The hash changed
IPFS is read-only
questions.correct_option: IPFS does not guarantee persistence unless the content is pinned/replicated
questions.explanation: IPFS is a network of providers; unpinned content can be garbage-collected.

Report cost and schedule health honestly.

• Hiding bad news until it is too late

stages.instruction:
Strategy is about what you will not do as much as what you will. Master prioritisation and you master the most critical PM skill.

OBJECTIVE
Set strategy and prioritise with clear frameworks.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Write a strategy
• Set OKRs
• Prioritise with a framework

stages.instruction:
Dart's null safety system is its most important modern feature — it eliminates an entire class of runtime errors. Understanding it from day one shapes good habits.

OBJECTIVE
Write correct, null-safe Dart with the right variable and collection types.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Use final and const correctly
• Handle null safely
• Choose appropriate collections

WORKED EXAMPLE
Write a CLI calculator. Step 1: read two numbers and an operator from input. Step 2: use a `switch` on the operator. Step 3: handle division by zero with a clear message rather than crashing. Step 4: loop until the user chooses to exit, and test each operation.

stages.instruction:
Flutter apps are inherently asynchronous — API calls, animations, user input. Understanding Dart's async model makes you a significantly better Flutter developer.

OBJECTIVE
Handle asynchronous work with Futures, Streams and isolates.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• Use async/await
• Consume a Stream
• Offload CPU work to an isolate

WORKED EXAMPLE
Fetch weather asynchronously. Step 1: make an HTTP request returning a `Future`. Step 2: `await` the response and decode the JSON. Step 3: map the fields into a typed model. Step 4: wrap the call in try/catch for network and parse errors and show a friendly message.

COMMON MISTAKES
• Blocking the main isolate with heavy work
• Not awaiting a Future and missing errors

stages.instruction:
AI is a broad field. Learn what modern AI tools actually do, how they differ from each other, and where they are genuinely useful versus where they are not the right tool.


LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Explain what modern AI systems can and cannot reliably do, and distinguish models, products, assistants, search tools, and agents.


TECHSKILLHUB LESSON
You are choosing, directing, and evaluating AI systems for everyday professional work. Understanding AI is about mental models and limits. The central idea is: Explain what modern AI systems can and cannot reliably do, and distinguish models, products, assistants, search tools, and agents. Do not treat AI output as the skill itself. The skill is the human ability to frame the problem, choose an appropriate AI role, inspect the result, and decide what happens next. Start with the required outcome and constraints, give only the context needed for that decision, and define how you will know whether the result is good enough.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Starting with a tool or prompt before defining the actual problem and success criteria.
• Treating a fluent or visually polished AI result as proof that it is correct or fit for purpose.
• Skipping an independent check when the output affects facts, code, money, privacy, safety, or other consequential decisions.
stages.worked_example: A customer asks for today’s market data. You first decide whether freshness requires search or a current-data source rather than relying on a model’s memory.

Treating a fluent or visually polished AI result as proof that it is correct or fit for purpose.
Skipping an independent check when the output affects facts, code, money, privacy, safety, or other consequential decisions.

resource_steps.description:
Take five realistic tasks and decide whether the first move should be AI, search, code/data tooling, automation, or human judgment.

INSTRUCTIONS
• Choose five tasks from your own work or study.
• For each task, name the tool category you would start with.
• Write one sentence explaining why a different tool would be weaker.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• You distinguish current-information tasks from generative tasks.
• You identify when computation or human judgment is more appropriate than a chatbot.
• Your reasoning is tied to the task requirements.

questions.question: A colleague says AI outputs are factual because models are trained on internet data. What is the best correction?
options: Training makes every output factual
Models learn patterns and generate outputs; factual reliability still requires verification
AI memorizes every webpage exactly
Search engines guarantee AI accuracy
questions.correct_option: Models learn patterns and generate outputs; factual reliability still requires verification
questions.explanation: Training enables pattern learning, not a guarantee that every generated claim is true.

questions.question: You receive a confident answer to a high-stakes question. What should you do?
options: Trust the confidence
Ask the model to promise accuracy
Identify what needs verification and check authoritative evidence
Publish it if the answer sounds professional
questions.correct_option: Identify what needs verification and check authoritative evidence
questions.explanation: Confidence and fluency are not evidence.

questions.question: You are given a new AI work task related to this stage. Which approach best demonstrates professional use of the stage competency?
options: Use the first AI output if it sounds confident
Define the task, success criteria, and constraints for the AI work problem before choosing how AI should help.
Add more adjectives to the prompt until the answer feels professional
Let the AI decide the success criteria after producing the output
questions.correct_option: Define the task, success criteria, and constraints for the AI work problem before choosing how AI should help.
questions.explanation: Professional AI use starts with the problem, constraints, and definition of success. The tool or prompt comes after the work is framed.

questions.question: Which evidence would give you the strongest confidence that someone actually understands this stage?
options: Whether the output is polished enough to avoid review
Whether the prompt was longer than the previous one
Look for evidence that the learner can explain generative ai in plain language, and can identify common failure modes rather than merely repeat a definition.
Whether the model generated the answer quickly
questions.correct_option: Look for evidence that the learner can explain generative ai in plain language, and can identify common failure modes rather than merely repeat a definition.
questions.explanation: Competence is shown through correct application, evidence, reasoning, and the ability to explain or improve the result—not by recognizing terminology.

questions.question: A learner completes the stage task but cannot explain why the result is reliable. What is the most appropriate next move?
options: Ask the learner to identify the success criteria, inspect the relevant evidence or failure modes, and revise the work.
Accept it because the output looks good
Give them the answer and mark the stage complete
Move them to the next stage because AI is probabilistic anyway
questions.correct_option: Ask the learner to identify the success criteria, inspect the relevant evidence or failure modes, and revise the work.
questions.explanation: A world-class pathway requires the learner to understand and evaluate the result, not merely produce an output.

stages.instruction:
The AI tool landscape is large and changing fast. Learn to categorize tools by what they do rather than by brand name, so you can choose the right one for any task.


LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Select AI tools based on the task, freshness requirements, evidence needs, modality, cost, and risk.


TECHSKILLHUB LESSON
You are choosing, directing, and evaluating AI systems for everyday professional work. The Modern AI Landscape is about tool selection. The central idea is: Select AI tools based on the task, freshness requirements, evidence needs, modality, cost, and risk. Do not treat AI output as the skill itself. The skill is the human ability to frame the problem, choose an appropriate AI role, inspect the result, and decide what happens next. Start with the required outcome and constraints, give only the context needed for that decision, and define how you will know whether the result is good enough.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Starting with a tool or prompt before defining the actual problem and success criteria.
• Treating a fluent or visually polished AI result as proof that it is correct or fit for purpose.
• Skipping an independent check when the output affects facts, code, money, privacy, safety, or other consequential decisions.

resource_steps.title: Practice: Practice: compare two AI tools for the same job
resource_steps.description:
Run the same clearly defined task through two different AI systems and compare the outputs instead of assuming one is universally better.

INSTRUCTIONS
• Choose a task that both tools can perform.
• Use the same useful context and output requirements.
• Compare accuracy, usefulness, limitations, and verification needs.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
• The task and evaluation criteria are explicit.
• You identify a meaningful difference between the tools.
• You make a task-specific recommendation.

questions.question: You need a current sourced answer about a fast-changing topic. What is the strongest approach?
options: Use any chatbot and trust its first answer
Use a tool suited to current research, inspect sources, and verify important claims
Use an older model
Avoid all AI
questions.correct_option: Use a tool suited to current research, inspect sources, and verify important claims
questions.explanation: Tool selection should reflect freshness, evidence needs, and consequences of error.

questions.question: Two AI tools give different answers. What should determine your choice?
options: Which sounds more confident
Task requirements, source quality, reliability, latency, and cost
Which has the best logo
Which answer is longer
questions.correct_option: Task requirements, source quality, reliability, latency, and cost
questions.explanation: Professional tool selection is evidence- and task-driven.

questions.question: You are given a new AI work task related to this stage. Which approach best demonstrates professional use of the stage competency?
options: Use the first AI output if it sounds confident
Add more adjectives to the prompt until the answer feels professional
Define the task, success criteria, and constraints for the AI work problem before choosing how AI should help.
Let the AI decide the success criteria after producing the output
questions.correct_option: Define the task, success criteria, and constraints for the AI work problem before choosing how AI should help.
questions.explanation: Professional AI use starts with the problem, constraints, and definition of success. The tool or prompt comes after the work is framed.

questions.question: Which evidence would give you the strongest confidence that someone actually understands this stage?
options: Look for evidence that the learner can compare at least two tool approaches, and can justify a tool choice using task requirements rather than merely repeat a definition.
Whether the output is polished enough to avoid review
Whether the prompt was longer than the previous one
Whether the model generated the answer quickly
questions.correct_option: Look for evidence that the learner can compare at least two tool approaches, and can justify a tool choice using task requirements rather than merely repeat a definition.
questions.explanation: Competence is shown through correct application, evidence, reasoning, and the ability to explain or improve the result—not by recognizing terminology.

questions.question: A learner completes the stage task but cannot explain why the result is reliable. What is the most appropriate next move?
options: Accept it because the output looks good
Give them the answer and mark the stage complete
Move them to the next stage because AI is probabilistic anyway
Ask the learner to identify the success criteria, inspect the relevant evidence or failure modes, and revise the work.
questions.correct_option: Ask the learner to identify the success criteria, inspect the relevant evidence or failure modes, and revise the work.
questions.explanation: A world-class pathway requires the learner to understand and evaluate the result, not merely produce an output.

stages.objective: Define team-level rules for AI-assisted development, including security, review, maintainability, and acceptable use.
stages.instruction:
Professional development with AI requires standards, review processes, and long-term thinking about maintainability.


LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Define team-level rules for AI-assisted development, including security, review, maintainability, and acceptable use.


TECHSKILLHUB LESSON
You are using AI inside a real software-development workflow where code still has to be understood, tested, reviewed, secured, and maintained. Professional AI-Assisted Development is about team policy. The central idea is: Define team-level rules for AI-assisted development, including security, review, maintainability, and acceptable use. Do not treat AI output as the skill itself. The skill is the human ability to frame the problem, choose an appropriate AI role, inspect the result, and decide what happens next. Start with the required outcome and constraints, give only the context needed for that decision, and define how you will know whether the result is good enough.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Starting with a tool or prompt before defining the actual problem and success criteria.
• Treating a fluent or visually polished AI result as proof that it is correct or fit for purpose.
• Skipping an independent check when the output affects facts, code, money, privacy, safety, or other consequential decisions.
stages.worked_example: A team defines acceptable AI usage, review gates, secret-handling rules, and documentation expectations.

stages.instruction:
Use AI to move from concept to prototype faster, while maintaining design quality and user focus.


LEARNING OBJECTIVE
Use prototypes to reduce the cost of learning before committing to full implementation.


TECHSKILLHUB LESSON
You are using AI to accelerate design exploration while keeping user needs, accessibility, consistency, evidence, and human judgment in control. Prototyping is about prototyping. The central idea is: Use prototypes to reduce the cost of learning before committing to full implementation. Do not treat AI output as the skill itself. The skill is the human ability to frame the problem, choose an appropriate AI role, inspect the result, and decide what happens next. Start with the required outcome and constraints, give only the context needed for that decision, and define how you will know whether the result is good enough.


COMMON MISTAKES
• Starting with a tool or prompt before defining the actual problem and success criteria.
• Treating a fluent or visually polished AI result as proof that it is correct or fit for purpose.
• Skipping an independent check when the output affects facts, code, money, privacy, safety, or other consequential decisions.
